docs.title: CUDA Hammer: A Tensor Compiler in C++
docs.text:
From a Minimal IR to Fused, Autotuned Kernels

Every tensor framework a reader has used -- PyTorch eager mode, a hand-written CUDA kernel, a NumPy script -- runs one operation at a time: allocate an output, launch a kernel, wait, move to the next line. That works, but it leaves real performance on the table in a specific, nameable way: every intermediate result round-trips through memory even when nothing outside the current computation ever needed it there, and every kernel launch pays its own fixed overhead regardless of how little work it does. A compiler that sees the whole computation graph before generating any code can fix both: fuse a chain of operations into one kernel so an intermediate value never leaves a register, and pick the loop tiling, ordering, and unrolling that the specific hardware it is targeting actually rewards. This book builds that compiler, called CUDA Hammer, from nothing -- no LLVM, no MLIR, no borrowed IR -- one real, working piece at a time.

This book is independent: it does not assume or reference any other book in any series, and it builds every piece of CUDA Hammer from Chapter 1 rather than pointing elsewhere for it. What it keeps is the same discipline its sibling books follow: every piece of code in this book is genuinely compiled, and wherever a real answer does not require hardware this book's own authoring environment does not have, it is genuinely run and checked against an independent reference. Where a claim depends on hardware this environment does not have -- a real GPU to execute CUDA Hammer's own generated CUDA kernels on -- that limitation is stated plainly rather than papered over with a fabricated number; Getting Started explains exactly where that line falls for this book.

docs.title: What this book covers
docs.text:
• Part 0 -- Why Compile Tensor Programs At All. The real, measurable cost of eager execution, what a general compiler pipeline actually looks like end to end, and a tour of how three real production ML compilers -- XLA, TVM, and Triton -- are actually built.
  • Part 1 -- CUDA Hammer's IR: A Minimal Tensor Graph From Scratch. Representing tensors and operations as a graph, a small frontend for building that graph, shape inference and validation, and tooling to print and visualize CUDA Hammer's own IR while developing it.
  • Part 2 -- Basic Optimization Passes. A real pass manager for structuring transformations, constant folding and dead code elimination, common subexpression elimination over a tensor graph, and algebraic simplification.
  • Part 3 -- Operator Fusion. Why fusion matters in the first place -- the real arithmetic-intensity argument behind memory-bound versus compute-bound kernels -- elementwise fusion, fusing reductions, loop fusion and tiling for the fused result, and precisely which fusion boundaries a real compiler cannot cross, and why.
  • Part 4 -- Code Generation. Lowering CUDA Hammer's high-level IR to an explicit loop nest, generating real CUDA C++ from the fused IR, generating real vectorized CPU code, and a JIT backend that compiles and loads generated code at runtime.
  • Part 5 -- Autotuning. The real search space a kernel's own schedule lives in (tile sizes, loop orders, unrolling), cost models versus genuine on-hardware measurement, building CUDA Hammer's own autotuner, and caching tuned schedules for reuse.
  • Part 6 -- Case Studies. How CUDA Hammer's own design choices compare to XLA's HLO fusion passes, TVM's Relay/TIR and Ansor auto-scheduling, Triton's block-level programming model, torch.compile and TorchInductor, Flash Attention read as a fusion case study, and quantization-aware code generation.

docs.title: How to read this book
docs.text: Every chapter follows the same shape: an intuition built from a concrete picture before any code, a background section with the real, complete implementation, one or more worked examples with genuinely computed output, a [COMMON TRAP] callout naming a specific, real mistake rather than a vague warning, a chapter summary, self-check questions, and worked solutions. Code that can genuinely run in this book's own authoring environment is genuinely run and its exact output locked into the page. Code whose correctness depends on hardware this environment does not have -- CUDA Hammer's own generated CUDA kernels, specifically -- is genuinely compiled for a real architecture and checked instead by a host-side reference implementation of the same computation; Getting Started explains this discipline in full.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This book builds CUDA Hammer entirely in C++17, with three real, distinct backends by the time Part 4 is done: a plain host C++ interpreter for CUDA Hammer's own IR (useful for testing a pass before trusting its output), a vectorized CPU code generator (real AVX2/FMA or NEON, whichever the machine actually has), and a CUDA C++ code generator that emits real kernels for nvcc. No external compiler framework -- no LLVM, no MLIR -- is used to build CUDA Hammer itself; Appendix C covers what a real production compiler gets by building on one of those instead, once CUDA Hammer's own from-scratch version exists to compare it against.

docs.title: Installing a toolchain
docs.text:
A working g++ (or clang++) supporting C++17 is all Part 0 through Part 3 need. Part 4 onward needs two more pieces, and this book is explicit about which of its own two authoring machines has which:

g++ --version      # C++17 host compiler, needed for everything
nvcc --version      # CUDA C++ compiler, needed from Chapter 18 onward

A CPU that actually supports AVX2 and FMA (check with grep avx2 /proc/cpuinfo on Linux, or sysctl -a | grep -i avx on Intel Mac) is what Chapter 19's x86 path needs to genuinely compile and run; a NEON-capable ARM CPU (essentially every Apple Silicon Mac and modern ARM server, confirmed by compiling and running a real <arm_neon.h> program against asimd in /proc/cpuinfo) is what its ARM path needs for the same. nvcc needs a CUDA toolkit install (apt-get install nvidia-cuda-toolkit on Debian/Ubuntu, or the installer from developer.nvidia.com) -- compiling for a target architecture with nvcc -arch=sm_XX never requires a matching physical GPU to be present, only to run the result.

docs.title: The honesty discipline this book follows
docs.text:
This book's own two authoring machines are, between them, real and different: a cloud sandbox (x86_64, real AVX2/AVX512F/FMA, real g++, real clang++, and a real, complete nvcc toolchain) and a connected device (aarch64, real NEON, real g++, no nvcc, no physical GPU on either machine). That split is treated as a feature, not a limitation to route around -- it means CUDA Hammer's CPU backend gets to be genuinely, fully honest in a way its GPU backend structurally cannot:

  • CUDA Hammer's IR, its pass manager, and its host-side interpreter (no vector intrinsics, no CUDA) are plain C++. They are genuinely compiled and genuinely run wherever they're touched, with exact output locked into the page and re-verified by a fresh recompile-and-rerun before publication.
  • CUDA Hammer's vectorized CPU backend (Chapter 19 onward) is genuinely compiled and genuinely run, for real, on two real, different architectures: AVX2/FMA intrinsics on the cloud sandbox, NEON intrinsics on the connected device. A claim about what fused, vectorized code actually computes is never simulated in this book -- it is measured directly, cross-checked bit-for-bit against a plain scalar reference, on real hardware, on two real instruction sets.
  • CUDA Hammer's CUDA backend (Chapter 18 onward) is genuinely compiled with nvcc for a real architecture (-arch=sm_80 unless a chapter says otherwise) and checked instead by a host-side reference implementation: ordinary C++ that computes the exact same result the generated kernel's own loop nest would, checked independently. This is the one honest limitation this book carries, stated once here rather than repeated on every page: neither authoring machine has a physical NVIDIA GPU, so a generated CUDA kernel's compiled correctness (does it build, does its PTX look right) is verified for real, but its runtime result is verified by the same reference implementation that was used to design it, not by executing the kernel itself.
  • Autotuning search and cost models (Part 5) are run for real against whichever backend a chapter is tuning -- the CPU backend's genuine on-hardware measurements are real, measured numbers; a CUDA-kernel cost model is a real, stated formula rather than a fabricated measured number, exactly like the sibling books' own standing rule against inventing timing data.
  • Real facts this book states about other compilers -- an XLA fusion rule, a TVM scheduling primitive, a Triton language feature -- are cited to that project's own real, current documentation or source, not asserted from memory.

Every chapter states which of the above applies to each piece of its own code, so nothing is left for a reader to guess about how a claim was actually established.

docs.title: Compile-line conventions
docs.text:
• Plain C++ host files (.cpp): g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -O2 file.cpp -o binary
  • AVX2/FMA CPU-codegen files: g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -mavx2 -mfma file.cpp -o binary (x86_64 only)
  • NEON CPU-codegen files: g++ -std=c++17 -O3 file.cpp -o binary (NEON is baseline on AArch64, no extra flag needed)
  • CUDA-generated files (.cu): nvcc -arch=sm_80 file.cu -o binary
  • A JIT-backend file that compiles and loads generated code at runtime shows its exact dlopen/linking recipe inline where it's introduced.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This book assumes working knowledge of C++ (classes, templates, smart pointers, RAII) and enough familiarity with how a tensor operation like matrix multiplication or a convolution is actually computed to follow why a particular fusion or tiling choice helps. No prior compiler-construction experience is assumed -- Part 0 builds the general vocabulary (IR, pass, lowering, codegen) from nothing before Part 1 ever starts building CUDA Hammer itself. No prior CUDA experience is assumed either; Chapter 18 introduces exactly the subset of the CUDA programming model CUDA Hammer's own generated kernels need, in place.
